title: Open Problem
body_md: Let $T$ be a positive operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$ with $\mathrm{r}(T)=1$. If $\lambda \in \sigma_{\mathrm{per}}(T)$, does it follow that $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T)$ for each $k \in \mathbb{Z}$?
head: environment
name: Cyclicity Conjecture

label: theorem:cyclicity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{theorem:cyclicity}
    Let $T$ be a positive operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$ such that $\mathrm{r}(T)=1$. Then $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T)$ for all $\lambda \in \sigma_{\mathrm{per}}(T)$ and $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

    Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a complex unital Banach algebra. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ be a connected open set and let $F \colon \Omega \to \mathcal{A}$ be holomorphic. Suppose that $\sigma(F(z)) \subseteq \overline{\mathbb{D}}$ for all $z \in \Omega$. Then $\sigma(F(z))\cap \mathbb{T}$ is independent of the choice of $z \in \Omega$.

label: proposition:rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity}
    Let $T$ be a positive operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$ with $\mathrm{r}(T) = 1$. Suppose that $T$ admits a minorant that is rotationally self-similar to it with respect to some $\lambda \in \mathbb{T}$. Then one has $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $S$ be a minorant of $T$ that is rotationally self-similar to $T$ with respect to $\lambda$. Then there exists a torsion operator $U$ on $E$ such that $SU = \lambda US$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:torsion-properties}(i), $U$ is an invertible isometry, so one has $\lambda S = U^{-1} S U$ and therefore $\lambda \sigma(S) = \sigma(S)$. Furthermore, since $S$ is positive and $\mathrm{r}(S) = 1$, one has $1 \in \sigma(S)$ by \cite[Proposition~V.4.1]{Schaefer1974}. Thus, it follows that $\lambda^k \in \sigma(S)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and Theorem~\ref{theorem:peripheral-domination} implies that $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T)$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:rotational-self-similarity-in-ultrapowers}
    Let $T$ be a positive operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$ with $\mathrm{r}(T) = 1$. Moreover, let $\mathcal{U}$ be a free ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $T$ admits a sequence of minorants that is asymptotically rotationally self-similar to it with respect to some $\lambda \in \mathbb{T}$. Then the operator $T^\mathcal{U}$ on $E^\mathcal{U}$ admits a minorant that is rotationally self-similar to it with respect to $\lambda$.

label: corollary:asymptotic-rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{corollary:asymptotic-rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity}
    Let $T$ be a positive operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$ with $\mathrm{r}(T) = 1$. If $T$ admits a sequence of minorants that is asymptotically rotationally self-similar to it with respect to some $\lambda \in \mathbb{T}$, then $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. By Proposition~\ref{proposition:rotational-self-similarity-in-ultrapowers}, $T^\mathcal{U}$ admits a minorant that is rotationally self-similar to it with respect to $\lambda$. Since $\mathrm{r}(T^\mathcal{U}) = \mathrm{r}(T) = 1$, Proposition~\ref{proposition:rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity} yields $\lambda^k \in \sigma(T^\mathcal{U}) = \sigma(T)$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Fix $\lambda \in \sigma_{\mathrm{per}}(T)$. Fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. We now pass to the space $\widehat E \coloneqq (E^\mathcal{U})''$ and the operator $\widehat T \coloneqq (T^\mathcal{U})''$. Then $\widehat E$ is Dedekind complete and $\widehat T$ is positive, since dual Banach lattices are Dedekind complete and adjoints of positive operators are positive (see \cite[Section~II.5]{Schaefer1974}). Moreover, spectra are preserved under passage to the bidual, so $\sigma(\widehat T) = \sigma(T^\mathcal{U}) = \sigma(T)$ and $\mathrm{r}(\widehat T) = 1$. Since $\lambda \in \partial\sigma(T) \subseteq \sigma_{\mathrm{app}}(T)$, one has $\lambda \in \sigma_p(T^\mathcal{U})$. The canonical embedding $J \colon E^\mathcal{U} \to (E^\mathcal{U})''$ satisfies $\widehat T J = J T^\mathcal{U}$, so $\lambda \in \sigma_p(\widehat T) \cap \mathbb{T}$. Thus, Proposition~\ref{proposition:asymptotically-rotationally-self-similar-minorants} implies that $\widehat T$ admits a sequence of minorants that is asymptotically rotationally self-similar to it with respect to $\lambda$. Corollary~\ref{corollary:asymptotic-rotational-self-similarity-implies-cyclicity} now yields $\lambda^k \in \sigma(\widehat T) = \sigma(T)$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, which proves the cyclicity conjecture in full generality.

label: proposition:signum-operator
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:signum-operator}
    Let $E$ be a complex Dedekind complete Banach lattice and let $x \in E$. Then there exists a unique complex-linear operator $S_x \colon E \to E$ satisfying the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)]
        \item $S_x \overline x = \abs x$, where $\overline x = \operatorname{Re} x - \mathrm{i} \operatorname{Im} x$.
        \item $\abs{S_x y} \leq \abs y$ for each $y \in E$.
        \item $S_x y = 0$ for each $y \in E$ such that $x \perp y$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $x = 0$, set $S_x = 0$. Otherwise, put $u \coloneqq \abs x$ and let $E_u \coloneqq \set{y \in E : \abs y \leq c u \text{ for some } c \geq 0}$ be the principal ideal generated by $u$. By \cite[Section~C-I.8]{NagelEd}, there exists a unique operator on $E_u$ satisfying (i) and (ii). This operator is order continuous and extends to the band $\set{u}^{\perp\perp}$ with the same domination by the order-continuous extension theorem for central operators (see the proof of \cite[Proposition~3.12(2)]{deJeu2025}). Since $E$ is Dedekind complete, this band is a projection band. Extending the operator by zero on $\set{u}^{\perp}$ yields the required operator $S_x$ on $E$. Finally, (ii) implies order continuity, so uniqueness follows from uniqueness on $E_u$, its order density in $\set{u}^{\perp\perp}$, and (iii).
head: environment

label: lemma:signum-properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:signum-properties}
    Let $E$ be a complex Dedekind complete Banach lattice and let $z \in E$. Let $P$ denote the band projection onto $\{\abs z\}^{\perp\perp}$. Then the following assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)]
        \item $S_z = S_zP$.
        \item $\abs{S_zx} = \abs x$ for each $x \in \{\abs z\}^{\perp\perp}$.
        \item $S_z \abs z = z$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof

label: proposition:torsion-properties
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{proposition:torsion-properties}
    Let $U$ be a torsion operator on a complex Banach lattice $E$. Then the following assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}[\upshape (i)]
        \item $U$ is an invertible isometry and $U^{-1} x = \overline{U \overline x}$ for all $x \in E$.
        \item $U$ is disjointness preserving, i.e., $U x \perp U y$ for all $x,y \in E$ with $x \perp y$.
        \item $U$ commutes with every band projection.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i): Clearly, $U$ is an isometry. For $0 < u \in E$, the principal ideal $E_u$ is invariant under $U$ and $\overline U$. With its gauge norm and order unit $u$, this ideal can be identified with a space $C(K)$ (see \cite[Section~II.7]{Schaefer1974}). Under this identification, $U$ is multiplication by the function $a \coloneqq U\operatorname{\mathbbm{1}}$: indeed, for $f \in C(K)$ and $t \in K$, the modulus identity applied to $f - f(t)\operatorname{\mathbbm{1}}$ gives $(Uf)(t) = a(t)f(t)$. Moreover, $\abs a = \operatorname{\mathbbm{1}}$, so $\overline U$ is multiplication by $\overline a$ and $U\overline U = \overline U U = I$ on $E_u$. Since every vector belongs to a principal ideal, these identities hold on $E$. Thus, $U^{-1} = \overline U$, and its inverse is again a torsion operator.

(ii): This follows immediately from $\abs{Ux} = \abs x$ and $\abs{Uy} = \abs y$.

(iii): The modulus identity implies that $U$ leaves every band invariant. If $P$ is a band projection, both $PE$ and $(I - P)E$ are therefore invariant under $U$, so $PU = UP$.
